rewrites.summary:
This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score, and the national framework is what a trans traveler stands under here. The 2012 gender identity law, allowing legal gender change without medical gatekeeping, remains on the books, so adult recognition and identity documents are not gated by medical approval.

Practical safety is the operative visitor concern: national hate-crime monitoring recorded 2025 as a record year with at least 227 bias-motivated crimes against LGBT people (up on 2024), one every 38 hours, physical violence forming the majority of cases (64.8%) and about a third occurring in police stations or penal institutions - the authorities-contact exposure a traveler meets on any police stop. No division-specific incident series, hostility mechanism or enforcement pattern is documented, so the visitor reads the national position without a local added risk factor.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-country policy turbulence, not local risk: the presidency eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry (a national ministry covering women, gender and diversity) and dismissed trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs for trans people; a presidential decree of 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatments. These are national-framework developments colouring any visit without creating a division-local mechanism.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data from the national monitoring: of the 227 recorded bias-motivated crimes in 2025, 62.5% of victims (142 people) were trans women or travestis, 18 trans men (against 5 in 2024), 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people, with police involvement rising from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025. The quota-law dismissals and the ministry's elimination fall mainly on trans residents employed in the public sector.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Both sources are national-framework pages, so no claim here verifies a division-local provision either way and provincial-level detail is unanchored. No visitor documents, border-screening practice or marriage/partner-travel provision specific to this division is recorded, and no freshness results are recorded for this division in the current wave.

rewrites.summary:
This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score, and the national framework is what a trans traveler stands under here. For a visitor the operative enforcement-relevant standards are detention-side: national law bars placing a person in a guarded centre wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence, and the framework was exercised in practice on 13 March 2024, when a court placed a transgender foreign woman (on hormone therapy since 2018) in a guarded centre for male foreigners, the border guard initially refused to move or release her despite the legal bar, and she was released only after a legal-aid association's application to the border-guard post commander.

On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that denying hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman in prison violated her right to private and family life and awarded damages, holding the refusal disproportionate with no reasonable legal grounds; the judgment binds the whole country and governs prison and detention healthcare in every voivodeship, including this one. No division-specific incident series, hostility mechanism or enforcement pattern is documented, so the visitor reads the national position without a local added risk factor.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National litigation flux colours the visit without dominating it: courts annulled municipal anti-LGBT declarations and the top administrative court upheld those annulments in May 2022 and on 28 June 2022, holding the resolutions violate the dignity of LGBT people and risk violence - a pattern running in the protective direction across the whole country. The municipalities of this voivodeship are recorded within that annulment history.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: the annulled declarations were municipal policy documents concerning local communities, and their annulment history sits within the resident legal environment. No resident-specific discrimination data, community-conduct practice or registry information for this voivodeship is on record in the packet's audited sources.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The audited sources address only detention standards; none covers passport-marker, border-screening, documents or marriage/partner-travel practice for trans travelers in this voivodeship. The municipal-declaration annulment history rests on the dossier's recorded text rather than this packet's audited sources. No trans-specific incident data for this voivodeship is on record; freshness entries for the detention pages are confirmed current, with the 2024 ruling standing and no reversing change through 2026.

blindSourceSummaries: Case report (13 March 2024): a court placed a transgender foreign woman who had been on hormone therapy since 2018 in a guarded centre for male foreigners, and the border guard refused to move or release her despite national law barring placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence; after a legal-aid association applied to the border-guard post commander she was released (page updated 28 March 2024). Establishes the current framework for trans foreigners in immigration detention - directly relevant to any trans visitor detained while in this state/province.

The judgment binds the country as a whole - the governing standard for trans people's healthcare in prisons and detention in every state/province, including this one.
